title: When Leaders Set Unrealistic Goals
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership field note separates healthy stretch from unachievable targets and argues that impossible goals damage the very people a leader hopes to inspire. Once a target moves from difficult to impossible, people stop trying to reach it and start trying to survive it, and the best performers disengage first. Unrealistic goals also invite corner-cutting, and the piece points to a large bank whose impossible targets produced millions of accounts customers never requested. Leaders tend to set such goals when they feel behind, because a bold number feels like action and stands in for the harder work of building a strategy. The recommended alternative is not aiming low: ask honestly whether the resources and talent exist, test goals with the people who must deliver them, and pair ambition with a credible path.
points: Impossible targets turn motivation into survival, and the strongest performers are usually the first to disengage.
Unattainable goals invite corner-cutting, because decent people with no honest path to success find a way to make results look better than they are.
Leaders most often set impossible goals when they feel behind, using a bold target as a substitute for a workable strategy.
Before setting a far-reaching goal, ask whether the resources and talent exist; if the honest answer is no, the goal is more wish than plan.
Test goals with the people who must deliver them and listen to pushback, pairing ambition with a path the team finds credible.
quotes: Once a target moves from difficult to impossible, people stop trying to reach it and start trying to survive it.
The best performers are typically the first to disengage. They refuse to run on a treadmill and expend effort without getting anywhere.
Worse yet, unrealistic goals invite people to cut corners. When failure is certain and the consequences are real, people find a way to make things look better than they are.
Such failures seldom begin with bad people. They begin with a goal that leaves decent people without an honest path to success.
A bold target feels like action and substitutes for the harder work of building a workable strategy.
Good leaders test goals with the people who must deliver them and listen when they push back.
The true measure of a goal is not how bold it sounds. It is whether people believe in it, commit to it, and can reach it with hard work.
